newsitem.title: USA: Networks will not delay declaring election winner.
newsitem.headline: Networks will not delay declaring election winner.

text.p: The major television networks Thursday rejected a request from Western states that they not declare a winner of the presidential election until polls close in the Pacific and Mountain time zones.
The four networks -- ABC, NBC, CBS and CNN -- said they had no plans to change the way they traditionally call the race on election night.
"We call them one at a time and when there is a clear winner," NBC spokeswoman Heidi Pokorny said, adding that the network would not wait for polls to close in the West.
She was responding to a letter sent by the secretaries of state of eight Western states asking the networks to withhold their projections until after polls close there, around midnight eastern time.

California's secretary of state, Bill Jones, said, "Turnout could be adversely affected if the national media starts projecting a winner prior to the closing of the polls in California." He was joined by his counterparts in Arizona, Idaho, Montana, Washington, Oregon, Utah and Nevada.

Roone Arledge, president of ABC News, said ABC would not predict the outcome of the election in any state "ahead of time." He said ABC would wait until a substantial number of polling places in a state had closed before calling the result.

"On the other hand, at a certain point, a president will have been elected, and it is foolish and naive to think that we can keep that a secret from the American people," he said on ABC's "World News Tonight" Wednesday.
CBS and CNN also said they had no intention of changing their election-night plans.
Using interviews with voters leaving the polls, the networks predict the vote in each of the 50 states, often before all polling stations are closed.

In 1980 the networks declared Ronald Reagan the winner over Jimmy Carter hours before polls closed, even in the East, lowering voter turnout in the West and causing networks to police themselves in subsequent elections.

But U.S. News and World Report magazine's "Washington Whispers" column this week speculated that an informal network agreement against rushing to be first to project a presidential winner was about to expire. The agreement was reached in 1990, when the networks began pooling exit polls.

Republican Party chairman Haley Barbour noted in a telephone news conference Tuesday that in 1992 it was not until about 10:40 p.m. EST, only 20 minutes before West Coast polls closed, that the networks said Bill Clinton had been elected president.
